results.title: GrokBot is amazing. Here's why I stopped using it.
results.content:
That paid off when it broke. The app's MCP server started cutting database reads off at 2,000 characters, so the board stopped refreshing, and I could see that it had. When a bot forgot a promise in chat, nothing changed, so nothing told me.

That app was Agent-Native Content, and Agent-Native is what my team builds at Builder. I'm biased, but that's also why I put my board there.

Agent-Native is our open-source framework for agentic apps. Mail, Content, Slides and Design each come with their own agent, built for one job, and an MCP server. You work in the app, and its agent, or any outside agent over MCP, works on the same state. [...] A general bot can hand the job to the app built for it, and you can open the app and see what happened. And because it's open source, when my board broke, I fixed that cutoff upstream myself.

GrokBot is amazing. It gave me a real week of what an always-on staff can do, and I want the version that lasts.

Agent-Native is one option among many. Whatever you build on, the split is the same: let models do the reasoning, the writing, and the coding, and leave the routing, the queues, the follow-ups, and the state to plain code. I paid $100 to learn that, so you don't have to.

Turn agent workflows into apps your team can use

Agent-Native is an open-source framework where people and agents work with the same actions and data.

Code the hard parts.

Offload the follow ups. [...] ## Why: GrokBot's own team explains it

Lee Robinson, who works on GrokBot at SpaceX, gave a Stanford lecture on how it's built, and it's a great, candid talk. Almost every complaint I had is on his slide of open problems.

Every wake is a model turn. Everything that can wake a bot (you, a routine, a webhook, another bot, background work finishing) goes through one router into that conversation's queue, one turn at a time. Then the model asks, in the slide's words, "Anything worth saying?" If not, "Quiet is allowed." Only one tool, SendToUser, ever reaches you.

That's a smart way to keep bots from being noisy. But it means silence costs a full model turn.

results.title: Grok is rated "Bad" with 1.4 / 5 on Trustpilot
results.content:
Grok/xAI has been one of the most frustrating and expensive AI services I have used. The marketing around SuperGrok and related plans promises substantial access, fewer restrictions than competitors, and useful tools for chat, research, image generation, and video. In practice the opposite is true. Subscriptions are costly—around $30 a month for SuperGrok and higher for other tiers—yet limits are so tight that even moderate daily use of text, images, or video exhausts weekly or daily allowances in a short time. Once the allowance is gone the service can lock completely, forcing either a long wait for reset (sometimes days) or payment of high extra fees for tiny additional amounts of usage. Free access is effectively useless. Limits have been tightened without clear advance notice, so [...] I accept that usage costs money. My complaint concerns spending visibility and the difficulty getting a meaningful human review when something goes wrong.  
  
AI acknowledgements and routing are fine. An automated loop that repeats policy without addressing the request for human escalation is an unacceptable support experience for a paying business customer.  
  
We are paying for both ChatGPT and Grok while evaluating whether to move more of our team across. This experience has seriously undermined my confidence in doing so.  
  
I want a named human to review the case, explain what the same usage would have cost under Ultra, and consider a fair refund or goodwill credit. I will update this review if the matter is resolved.
